hooks.text: Earth's shadow almost never touches the Moon.
The Moon’s phases have nothing to do with Earth’s shadow.
Humans have tracked the Moon for 10,000 years while misunderstanding it.

title: The 10,000-Year Moon Shadow Myth
description: Discover why the changing phases of the Moon are actually a trick of perspective rather than Earth's shadow.

beats.text: Earth's shadow almost never touches the Moon.
beats.visual: NASA photography of a bright full moon showing near side features

beats.text: For 10,000 years since Warren Field in Scotland, humans tracked this cycle while misunderstanding it.
beats.visual: Warren Field archaeological site pits in Scotland

beats.text: This site beat every other ancient calendar to become the world's oldest formal record of time.
beats.visual: Illustration of the Mesolithic pit alignment at Warren Field

beats.text: That ancient pit calendar recorded the phases, but Earth was never blocking the Sun.
beats.visual: Moon phases diagram showing Sun illumination by NASA

beats.text: In reality, the Sun constantly illuminates exactly half of the Moon's rocky surface.
beats.visual: Lunar orbit geometry diagram showing Sun and Earth

beats.text: As the Moon orbits every 29.5 days, our perspective of that sunlit side constantly shifts.
beats.visual: First quarter moon telescope image showing the terminator line

beats.text: Our planet's massive shadow only touches the lunar surface during rare eclipses twice a year.
beats.visual: Total lunar eclipse blood moon by NASA

beats.text: Yet despite millennia of human record-keeping, millions still believe that Earth creates these shadows.
beats.visual: Artist concept of Earth casting a shadow toward the Moon

beats.text: This explains why Earth's shadow almost never touches the Moon.
beats.visual: High resolution video of moon phases cycling through a month

better_than_last: Applied the record structure to highlight the Warren Field calendar as the historical anchor while ensuring the final beat is a complete sentence that loops perfectly.
